text: With delivery trucks constantly under attack, Venezuela's food now moves under armed guard. Soldiers keep watch over bakeries. They forced open a large metal gate and streamed inside. They grabbed water, flour, cornmeal, salt, sugar, potatoes, whatever they could find, leaving nothing behind but broken freezers and overturned shelves. Known as the “Caracazo,” or the “Caracas clash,” the riots were triggered by low oil prices, subsidy cuts and a population that had suddenly become impoverished. The episode seared the memory of a future president, Hugo Chávez, who said the country's failure to provide for its people, and the state's repression of the uprising, were the reasons Venezuela needed a socialist revolution. Now his successors are caught in a similar bind, or perhaps an even worse one. The nation is anxiously looking for ways to feed itself.

title: Trump inauguration set to be low-key despite his showman image
text: Donald Trump built his name on opulent hotels and a dramatic reality TV show, but his inauguration on Friday as the 45th U.S. president is shaping up to be a more subdued event, with major entertainment stars staying away. As his predecessors did, Trump will take the oath of office on the steps of the U.S. Capitol building and lead a parade down Pennsylvania Avenue, but there will be fewer official balls and less glitz and celebrity talent to greet the new president. Inaugurations have been star-studded events since 1941, when President Franklin Roosevelt held a gala with actors Charlie Chaplin, Mickey Rooney and other stars of the time, said Jim Bendat, a historian who has written a book on U.S. inaugurations. This year, however, several singers, including Elton John and Charlotte Church, turned down invitations to perform at inaugural events. Trump, a New York businessman and former star of the “The Apprentice” TV show, won on a populist platform that included pledges to build a wall along the Mexican border, restrict immigration from Muslim countries and dismantle Obamacare. Broadway star Jennifer Holliday agreed to perform but pulled out after a backlash from fans. “You can’t really find precedent for that,” Bendat said in an interview. The Mormon Tabernacle Choir, singer Jackie Evancho and the Rockettes dance troupe are among the scheduled performers, although individual Rockettes will be allowed to opt out if they choose. Trump's inaugural committee has said it is deliberately avoiding top entertainers. “We’re fortunate in that we have the greatest celebrity in the world, which is the president-elect,” Tom Barrack, the inaugural committee chairman, told reporters at Trump Tower in New York last week.

title: Marco Rubio's campaign strategy is a real puzzle
text: Something is strange about Marco Rubio's presidential campaign: he hasn't been doing much, well, campaigning in the early states. Most recent winners of presidential nominations put serious time and effort into campaigning and building organizations in at least one of Iowa or New Hampshire, but Rubio has taken a decidedly relaxed approach to both. He rarely shows up, does little campaigning when he is there, and doesn't appear to be building very impressive field operations. And people are noticing. James Pindell of the Boston Globe wrote last week that Rubio's New Hampshire surge was "riddled with doubts," and that GOP insiders are bemoaning his "lack of staff" and "activity." National Review's Tim Alberta and Eliana Johnson reported Wednesday that Rubio's "weak ground game" was angering Iowa Republicans. And the New Hampshire Union Leader wrote an editorial headlined, "Marco? Marco? Where's Rubio?" For a candidate so often labeled "The Republican Barack Obama," Rubio sure seems to have missed some key lessons from the president's historic 2008 campaign. It is also bad optics for a candidate who has already been criticized (somewhat unfairly) for missing lots of Senate votes. The conventional wisdom holds that a candidate must win either Iowa or New Hampshire to win the nomination. Indeed, every nominee for decades has done so, except Bill Clinton in 1992 (an unusual year in which the Iowa caucuses effectively "didn't count" because Iowan Tom Harkin was running). Candidates who have tried to "skip" both early states, hoping a later win would propel them to prominence, have failed miserably. The same conventional wisdom also says that the way to win in Iowa and New Hampshire is to work hard on the ground. The candidate should spend a lot of time there.

title: Republicans launch final drive to scrap Obama-era regulations
text: Lawmakers, lobbyists and interest groups are making a last push in their battle over regulations put in place during former President Barack Obama's final months in office, with the financial services industry working hard to eliminate a rule on retirement plans run by states. Relying on an obscure 1996 law called the Congressional Review Act, Republicans have passed 13 resolutions killing Obama-era regulations on energy, the environment, gun control, education, family-planning funding and corruption. Once rules are eliminated, agencies can never create “substantially similar” regulation. The deadline for introducing new CRA resolutions on regulations enacted under Obama passed nearly a month ago, and Republicans are working to finish resolutions already in the legislative pipeline before the third week of May. For now, the resolutions need only simple majorities in both houses of Congress to reach President Donald Trump for his signature. After May 11, they will need 60 votes in the Senate to pass, a steep hurdle, given that voting margins on CRA resolutions have been tight and Vice President Mike Pence had to break a tie on one. A spokeswoman for Speaker Paul Ryan said the House of Representatives will probably hold no more CRA votes. A spokesman for Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell said McConnell “has expressed interest in considering more” resolutions. The resolution on state-run retirement plans has been stuck in limbo for weeks. Obama's Labor Department had exempted both state- and city-run retirement plans from the 1974 Employee Retirement Income Security Act, or ERISA, a law meant to protect workers' savings through detailed compliance requirements.

title: Health insurer lobby asks for delay in 2018 Obamacare deadline
text: The biggest lobbying group for health insurers has asked U.S. lawmakers who are weighing Obamacare's fate to push back the deadline for 2018 individual insurance submissions to regulators, hoping to get greater clarity on the program's future later on. Republican leaders including President-elect Donald Trump and U.S. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell have said they want to repeal President Barack Obama's signature health insurance program, the Affordable Care Act, which provides coverage to millions of Americans. Trump has said some parts of the program are good, such as letting young adults stay insured with their parents until age 26. The trade association America's Health Insurance Plans, or AHIP, has been talking with senators for the past few weeks, spokeswoman Kristine Grow said on Tuesday. She provided a list of issues being discussed, which relate to the individual exchanges, Medicare and Medicaid. Insurers supported the idea of high-risk pools, saying they can reduce the risk of adverse selection and provide effective coverage. Both Trump and his pick to lead the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Tom Price, favor using the pools to insure the very sick. Two of AHIP's largest members, Anthem Inc and Cigna Corp, both plan to sell Obamacare plans in 2017. Insurers also asked for funding through Jan. 1, 2019, for cost-sharing programs and for the 2016 reinsurance payments to qualifying insurers to be made as planned. And they asked for two health insurance taxes to be eliminated, which they said would help slow premium growth.

title: Libyans trade jewelry for medical care as crisis deepens
text: In a square behind Libya's central bank, black market dealers, some of them armed, carry small plastic bags of dollars and larger ones of dinars in and out of one of many informal exchanges. Traders import food and other goods at the official rate and sell them at the unofficial one, pocketing huge profits; others make similarly large sums smuggling out heavily subsidized fuel. Meanwhile, in the back streets of the old city, ordinary people have turned to selling jewelry or dollars hidden at home as six years of post-dictatorship chaos take their toll. "I haven't been paid for four months," said Fatima, 40, from the southern city of Sabha, as she sold three small gold charms to pay for diabetes treatment for her sister, Hasina, who added: "We're helpless, there's nothing else we can do." In other signs of growing poverty, elderly women beg drivers for cash on Tripoli's streets and families line up for charity food handouts. The U.N. estimated that about 1.3 million people in Libya need humanitarian assistance this year. Their situation worsened again over the past two weeks after the black market rate of the dinar, long stuck at record lows, slid further, fuelling inflation that is already around 25-30 percent. The central bank blamed the audit bureau and the U.N.-backed government for restricting letters of credit that pay for basic supplies to a divided country where a security vacuum and smuggling networks have destabilized the wider region. Officials had come across suspicious requests, including one to import tuna worth $120,000, more than the country consumes in a year, according to a Libyan entrepreneur who declined to be named for fear of retribution from Libya's powerful armed groups.

title: Most Americans support military action against North Korea: Gallup poll
text: Most Americans back military action against North Korea if economic and diplomatic efforts fail, according to a Gallup poll released on Friday amid mounting tension over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons program and recent missile launches. The survey of 1,022 U.S. adults last week found that 58 percent would favor military action against North Korea if the United States cannot first achieve its goals by more peaceful means. That support, however, was largely divided along party lines. Among Republicans, 82 percent would support military action, compared with 37 percent of Democrats. Among political independents, 56 supported such action. Half still believe the situation can be resolved through sanctions and diplomacy, and most Americans doubt any U.S. military attack is imminent in the next six months, Gallup said. The findings came as North Korea fired another missile over Japan earlier on Friday, according to South Korean and Japanese officials. "A majority of Americans appear ready to support military action against that country, at least as a last resort," Gallup wrote in its report. But, it added, "Americans still think North Korea is bluffing." The results marked a shift from 2003, when Gallup last asked about U.S. support for military action against Pyongyang and 47 percent said they supported it. Most of the change was among Republicans and independents, it added. A sharp rise in support among Republicans, possibly reflecting President Donald Trump's promise to respond with fire and fury to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un's threats, accounts for much of this, Gallup said. In August, Trump warned North Korea it would face fire and fury if it threatened the United States. The survey was conducted by telephone interviews between Sept. 6 and Sept.

title: Mexican families urge their 'Dreamer' children to keep fighting
text: Yolanda Varona is urging her children and thousands of other young Mexicans who may lose their right to live in the United States to stay and fight for their American Dream. Varona is the mother of two of the 800,000 people, most of them Mexican, who could face deportation after U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday ended the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program (DACA). DACA gave work permits to people known as Dreamers who were brought to the United States illegally as children by immigrants such as Varona. Trump scrapped the Obama-era program but put off implementation until March to give Congress time to draft an alternative. After Varona was deported in 2010 and separated from her two children in the United States, she set up a chapter of Dreamers Moms in the border city of Tijuana. The Tijuana chapter has 80 mothers whose children in the United States could lose the legal protection that originally persuaded them to risk registering with the U.S. government to join DACA. "We want them to keep fighting, they can achieve better things there," Varona said by telephone. "In the unfortunate case that the police arrive to deport them, we will be there to help them." Varona said Trump's decision would push young people back into living in the shadows. She stressed how hard it was for these young people to return to Mexico, where they have lost family ties and sometimes do not speak the language. Some 625,000 young Mexicans are enrolled under DACA.
